title: Biggest Rise to a Later Value
statement:
You get an array nums. Pick two positions i < j where the later value is strictly larger: nums[i] < nums[j]. The rise is nums[j] − nums[i].

Return the largest rise you can find. If no pair has a strictly larger later value, return -1.

examples.why: 3 then 9 rises by 6. The 1 is the smallest value, but only 6 comes after it, a rise of 5.
Values never go up. The two 7s are equal, which does not count as a rise.
The best pair uses the minimum so far (1) and a value that comes much later (10); they are not neighbours.

hints: Fix the later position j. Which earlier value gives it the biggest rise?
The smallest value seen before j. Keep that running minimum as you scan from left to right.
At each j, if nums[j] is strictly bigger than the running minimum, update the answer; then update the minimum. Start the answer at −1.

explain.intuition:
For any later position j, the best partner is simply the smallest value somewhere before it. So one left-to-right scan is enough: carry the minimum so far, and at each step ask how much the current value rises above it.

This is the same shape as "buy low, sell high later". You never need the pair itself, only the cheapest point behind you.
steps: For each j from 1: if nums[j] > low, set best = max(best, nums[j] − low).
pitfalls: Taking the global maximum minus the global minimum. The maximum may come before the minimum.
Starting best at 0. Equal values give a rise of 0, which is not allowed: the answer must be -1 then.
Only comparing neighbours. The best pair is often far apart.

solutions.title: Every pair
solutions.idea: Try every i < j and keep the largest strictly positive difference.

solutions.title: Running minimum
solutions.idea: The best partner for each later value is the smallest value before it.

followups: Return the pair of positions too, preferring the earliest i on ties.
You may make several non-overlapping rises and add them up. What is the best total?
